H1.text: Push an empty trolley, and it shoots ahead. Push a full one just as hard, and it barely moves.

H2.text: Kick a ball softly, then hard. One rule decides all of this.

H3.text: Aarav pushes his bicycle out of the college gate. Then a friend sits on the carrier, and he pushes just as hard.

H4.text: Empty, the bike leaps forward. With his friend, it crawls. Exactly how much slower?

H5.text: One rule answers that, to the decimal. Let's build it.

P1.text: Newton's second law links three things.

P2.text: The net force on a body, its mass, and its acceleration.

P3.text: Net force means all the pushes and pulls, added with their directions.

P4.text: Push a box with thirty newtons to the right, while friction pulls back with ten. The net force is twenty newtons, right.

P5.text: Mass is how much matter a body has, in kilograms. More mass is harder to speed up.

S1.text: To the motion notebook. A two kilogram cart on a smooth track, no friction.

S2.text: Pull it with two newtons. Its velocity grows steadily. The acceleration is one metre per second squared.

S3.text: Double the pull to four newtons. The acceleration doubles too, to two.

S4.text: Six newtons gives three. On the graph, the dots sit on a straight line through zero. a is proportional to F.

S5.text: Now keep six newtons, and add mass. At four kilograms, the acceleration halves, to one point five.

S6.text: At six kilograms, just one. Three times the mass, one third of the acceleration.

S7.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze, and draw the arrows.

S8.text: The orange force arrow and the red acceleration arrow point the same way. The blue velocity arrow grows along them.

S9.text: One last run. Six newtons on the bare cart. Watch the moment we let go.

S10.text: Your turn. The moment the push stops, what is the cart's acceleration? Pause and decide.

S11.text: Zero, at once! No net force, no acceleration. The cart does not stop.

S12.text: Watch. The force goes, a drops to zero, and v stays at three metres per second.

D1.text: Now let's write the rule, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Keep the mass fixed. a is proportional to F.

D3.text: Step two. Keep the force fixed. a is proportional to one over m.

D4.text: Step three. Together, a is proportional to F over m. So F equals k, m, a, with k a constant.

D5.text: Step four. We pick the unit of force so that k is exactly one. So F equals m a.

D6.text: Step five. One newton gives one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared. So one newton is one kilogram metre per second squared.

D7.text: F is the net force, and a points along it. Newton first wrote this law with momentum. That form comes in episode fifty four.

T1.text: Remember this. Net force equals mass times acceleration.

K1.text: Side by side. The same five kilogram box. Ten newtons gives two metres per second squared. Twenty gives four.

K2.text: Now ten newtons on a ten kilogram box. The acceleration drops to one. More mass, less acceleration.

K3.text: Now you try. Double the force, and double the mass too. What happens to the acceleration? Pause and decide.

K4.text: It stays the same! a is F over m. Twice the force over twice the mass is the same ratio.

W2.text: Aarav and his bike have a mass of eighty kilograms. He pedals with one sixty newtons, and friction and air push back with forty. Find his acceleration, and his speed after four seconds.

W3.text: First, the net force. One sixty forward, minus forty back. One hundred and twenty newtons, forward.

W4.text: Then a equals F over m. One twenty divided by eighty is one point five metres per second squared.

W5.text: From rest, v equals a t. One point five times four is six metres per second.

W6.text: Now the hook. With his seventy kilogram friend, the mass is one fifty. The same net force gives only zero point eight.

X2.text: Many students put the push alone into F equals m a. Fifty newtons on a ten kilogram box gives five.

X3.text: But friction pulls back with twenty. F in this law is the net force. Thirty newtons over ten kilograms gives three.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In questions that find acceleration from the net force, on blocks, ropes and lifts.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A constant force acts on a two kilogram body for four seconds. Its velocity goes from four i plus three j, to minus four i minus three j. Find the size of the force. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Five newtons.

A2.text: The change in velocity is minus eight i, minus six j. Its size is ten metres per second.

A3.text: So the acceleration is ten over four, two point five metres per second squared.

A4.text: F equals m a, two times two point five, five newtons. The speed stayed five, but the velocity reversed.

Y2.text: One. The same push on an empty bike and a loaded bike. Which speeds up more, and why?

Y3.text: Two. What is one newton, in base units?

Y4.text: Three. Why must F in F equals m a be the net force?
